clinicalPearls: Weakness of the lateral rectus causes horizontal binocular diplopia worse at distance and on gaze toward the affected side
The affected eye is esotropic and fails to abduct fully beyond the midline in a complete palsy
Because the sixth nerve has a long intracranial course it is a poor localiser and can be a false-localising sign of raised intracranial pressure
Common causes include microvascular ischaemia, raised intracranial pressure, tumour, trauma and cavernous sinus disease
In children, a post-viral benign sixth nerve palsy occurs but a posterior fossa tumour must be excluded
Bilateral or progressive palsies and any additional neurological signs mandate neuroimaging
reference.pathophysiology: The abducens nerve supplies the lateral rectus, so its dysfunction impairs abduction and leaves the eye deviated inward by the unopposed medial rectus. Its long course from the pons, up the clivus, over the petrous apex and through the cavernous sinus makes it vulnerable along many segments; stretching from raised intracranial pressure explains its false-localising behaviour. Microvascular ischaemia of the nerve, as in diabetes and hypertension, is a frequent self-limiting cause, whereas compressive, inflammatory or infiltrative lesions produce more persistent or progressive palsies.
additionalDifferentials: Thyroid eye disease with restricted medial rectus
Medial orbital wall fracture with muscle entrapment
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and orbits, including the cavernous sinus and skull base
Assessment for papilloedema and features of raised intracranial pressure
Acetylcholine-receptor antibody testing if myasthenia is suspected
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure when intracranial hypertension is suspected
redFlags: Papilloedema or other signs of raised intracranial pressure
Additional cranial neuropathies or long-tract signs
Associated severe headache or systemic features
reference.prognosis: Isolated microvascular palsies usually recover within weeks to a few months; other causes depend on the underlying pathology, and persistent deviation may need prism or strabismus surgery.
pitfalls: Assuming a microvascular cause and missing raised intracranial pressure
Overlooking a posterior fossa tumour in a child
Mistaking restrictive or myasthenic limitation for a neurogenic palsy
Failing to re-image a palsy that does not recover as expected
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Identify and treat the underlying cause, optimising vascular risk factors such as diabetes and hypertension for a microvascular palsy and addressing raised intracranial pressure, tumour, inflammation or cavernous-sinus pathology directly
Relieve troublesome binocular diplopia symptomatically with monocular occlusion or patching, or a Fresnel prism, during recovery
Observe presumed microvascular palsies, which typically recover spontaneously over weeks to a few months
Investigate promptly with neuroimaging and refer any bilateral, progressive, paediatric or non-isolated palsy, or one failing to recover, to exclude serious intracranial pathology
Treat raised intracranial pressure on its merits, for example acetazolamide and weight management in idiopathic intracranial hypertension or neurosurgical intervention, when it is the cause
Consider botulinum toxin to the antagonist medial rectus, or strabismus surgery, for persistent deviation that does not resolve
